content.jointProblem: Can thermo-mechanical stress analysis and targeted changes to potting materials, interfaces or enclosure geometry reduce KL-HSM epoxy cracking while preserving tamper evidence? The first experiment would characterize the actual epoxy and reproduce baseline cracking under the company's thermal-cycle protocol to test whether Erić's steel-based experimental and modelling methods transfer to this assembly, before testing candidate changes against the proposed 200-cycle target.

rationale.text: Erić has directly relevant experience investigating interactions between thermal cycling, mechanical loading and crack development, although demonstrated on welded steel rather than epoxy assemblies.

sources.quote: Crack growth rates in both TMF programmes exceeded predictions based on simple superposition of mechanical and thermal stress intensities

rationale.text: His work combines temperature-dependent finite-element models with experimental deformation measurements, providing a methodological basis for investigating local stress concentrations in the enclosure.

sources.quote: FE simulations using temperature-dependent elastic–plastic material models reproduced the crack-tip opening displacement within 8% of experimental digital image correlation measurements.

rationale.text: He has led experimental testing and simulation within a collaborative structural-integrity project.

sources.quote: Erić led the experimental testing and simulation activities on the Serbian side and co-supervised a doctoral student enrolled at Zagreb.

constraints.text: Candidate assemblies must be tested across −10°C to 60°C against the company's proposed target of 200 cycles without visible fracturing; this is an acceptance target to investigate, not an assured result.

sources.quote: Our target operating range for the certified product is -10°C to 60°C.
A good outcome is an enclosure that passes 200 thermal cycles without visible fracturing.

constraints.text: Changes must preserve the required tamper evidence and fit the seven-month window before scheduled physical evaluation; fracture resistance alone is not the certification objective.

sources.quote: Common Criteria EAL4+ requires that our KL-HSM enclosure demonstrate tamper evidence under physical stress, including thermal cycling.
the physical testing phase is scheduled to begin in seven months.

constraints.text: Diagnosis must use the available samples, four test runs and enclosure drawings, and explicitly represent the PCB corners and metal–potting interfaces where cracking occurs.

sources.quote: We have physical samples, test data from the last four test runs, and the enclosure drawings available.
The fractures appear near the corners of the PCB substrate and at points where metallic fasteners meet the potting compound.

constraints.text: The project must have a tightly defined, practically applicable scope compatible with the company's modest collaboration capacity.

sources.quote: with modest capacity to take on collaborative projects if the scope is well-defined and the output is practically applicable.

constraints.text: Extended testing requires advance reservation of the researcher's shared climate chamber and fatigue equipment.

sources.quote: Erić's climate chamber and servo-hydraulic machine are shared with two other research groups; scheduling access for extended test campaigns requires advance coordination.

risks: The documented fracture and thermal-cycling methods concern steel, not cured epoxy, PCB substrates or polymer–metal adhesion. Their transfer is unvalidated; the first experiment must establish actual epoxy behaviour and baseline assembly cracking before relying on model predictions.
No polymer-specific expertise or Common Criteria evaluation experience is established in the researcher's material. A polymer specialist and the accredited laboratory may need to participate.
A formulation or geometry change could suppress visible cracking while weakening tamper evidence; passing 200 thermal cycles alone would not establish certification readiness.

Researcher availability is explicitly unknown. Shared equipment access, unconfirmed chamber suitability for the complete −10°C to 60°C protocol, and material-characterization work could compromise the seven-month schedule.
Project budget, sample quantities, supplier material-data access and permission to change formulations or enclosure features are unknown.
The company gives both a relative seven-month testing window and an end-of-2025 certification plan; the current evaluation dates need confirmation.
questions: Can Erić commit time to this epoxy-focused joint project, and can a polymer/adhesion specialist join if required?
What are the current laboratory dates, intermediate design-freeze deadlines and agreed tamper-evidence acceptance criteria?
What thermal ramp rates, dwell times, humidity, assembly constraints and inspection methods produced the existing failures, and how is 'visible fracturing' defined?
Can the supplier provide formulation and cured-material property data, and are retained samples and process records available for both tested epoxies?
How many representative enclosures and test coupons can be supplied, and which changes to potting, fasteners, PCB corners or interfaces are permitted?
Can suitable thermal-cycling and polymer-characterization equipment be booked early enough, including confirmed operation at 60°C and space for representative assemblies?
What budget and company engineering time are available, and what confidentiality and data-access arrangements apply to enclosure drawings and security-sensitive samples?
